points.description: Reformulation (or equivalent use of A(x)=2x-floor(2x)): n(n+1)r - B(n,r) = sum_{k=1}^n floor(2kr), so the condition is n | sum_{k=1}^n floor(2kr) for all n. Any correct equivalent handling earns the mark.
Verifies that every positive integer r works: 2kr is an integer, so A(kr)=0, B=0, and n(n+1)r is a multiple of n. Must be stated for all positive integers r.

Rational case: proves that a rational r that is not an integer fails, by exhibiting a suitable n (for example n=2 kills half-integers, and a general argument, e.g. with n tied to the denominator or via differences of consecutive sums, for other fractions). A valid complete argument is needed; checking only a few examples earns at most 1 mark.

levels.says: Handles only some rational cases (e.g. half-integers or specific denominators) or the argument has a gap.

points.description: Irrational case: proves that irrational r fails (e.g. using the n-th and (n-1)-th conditions to show floor(2nr) ≡ a congruence that forces 2r rational/integer, or an equidistribution/fractional-part argument). Valid alternative arguments accepted. A unified argument covering all non-integer real r earns this mark and P3.

levels.says: Sketch of the right idea for irrationals but with a significant gap.

points.description: States the final answer: exactly the positive integers r.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the reformulation, verification that integers work, a proof that non-integers (rational and irrational) fail, and the answer "all positive integers". Giving only the answer with integer check earns about 2-3 marks. Do not give credit for the claim that half-integers work; r=1/2 fails at n=2.
rubric.answer_key: Since A(x)=2x-floor(2x), B(n,r)=n(n+1)r - sum_{k=1}^n floor(2kr). So the condition is n | sum_{k≤n} floor(2kr) for all n. If r is a positive integer, every term A(kr)=0, so n(n+1)r - 0 is a multiple of n: works. Conversely, if r is not an integer, the divisibility fails for some n (e.g. r=1/2: n=2 gives 3, not a multiple of 2; in general rationals with denominator issues and irrationals are excluded by the sum conditions). Answer: all positive integers r.
